newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish ruling ex-communists back Britain's Blair.
newsitem.headline: Polish ruling ex-communists back Britain's Blair.

text.p: Poland's ruling ex-communists rooted for British Labour leader Tony Blair during their traditional May Day march through Warsaw on Thursday.

"Good luck, Tony Blair" proclaimed a long red banner carried by young activists of the Social Democratic (SdRP) party, which was born from the ashes of the Polish United Workers' Party (PZPR) after the 1989 fall of communism.
They also carried a large portrait of Blair, whose party is widely expected to win Britain's May 1 parliamentary election, making him prime minister.

Up to 2,000 members of leftist groups including the Social Democrats, dominant force in Poland's coalition government, marched to the sound of a brass band, braving shouted insults and tomatoes flung by radical right-wing opposition supporters.
While the hecklers chanted demands for the former communists to face trial and occasionally scuffled with police, the leftists on the march flung back shouts of "fascists".

The SdRP, which now supports democracy, fast European Union and NATO membership and market economics, sees itself as a Western-style social democratic party and has forgiven itself for its undemocratic communist antecedents.
One SdRP supporter carrying the pro-Blair banner told Reuters it was hard to pinpoint differences between Britain's two big parties as ideology was going out of politics.

"But what is important is the symbolism, where the Labour party sprang from," youth activist Marta Jarosinska said, adding that a Labour victory after years of Conservative rule would deliver a startling message to the rest of Europe.

A theme of the small May Day march -- a far cry from the orchestrated Soviet-style parades held until 1980 when the free Solidarity union emerged -- was support for a draft Polish constitution which will be put to a nationwide referendum on May 25.

This draft, a compromise reached between the ruling coalition and two opposition parties in parliament, is designed to replace the defunct 1952 document which was amended by an interim constitution following the collapse of communism.
It is strongly opposed by the rightist opposition grouped around Solidarity which has prepared its own draft reflecting the values of Roman Catholicism, Poland's majority religion.

In the central city of Lodz, private Radio Zet reported that police detained several rightists who had been preparing to satirise a leftist gathering, while in Poznan in the west there were scuffles between counter-demonstrators and police.
Some Solidarity union supporters around the country marked the traditional workers' holiday with church services in honour of St Joseph the Worker.
